fields.h1: Build a Compensation Survey and Own the Pay Data
fields.hero_description: Build a compensation survey that matches jobs by description, checks each salary entered, and saves it to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What the Survey Handles Before the Report
fields.features_subheading: What Emergent builds behind a compensation survey, and what stays yours once the survey closes.
fields.feature_1:
Questions drafted from your job list

List the jobs you want to compare and the pay you need for each. Emergent drafts the survey, one section per job, and you change any question by typing a follow-up prompt.
fields.feature_2:
Each job matched by its description

Participants read a short description beside each benchmark job and pick the role in their firm that does that work. Their own job title never has to match the one on your list.
fields.feature_3:
Pay data in a database you own

Each entry lands as a row in a database you own: firm, job, headcount, base pay, bonus, and effective date. Filter by region or firm size before any figure leaves the table.
fields.feature_4:
Reminders until every participant submits

Participants that miss the deadline get an email reminder, and your team gets a Slack alert naming each one still out. Anyone who has already submitted gets no further emails.
fields.feature_5:
No cap on responses

Emergent puts no cap on survey responses. A council with 400 member firms collects every submission, and a staff survey at a 3,000-person company reaches every employee.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain, and the code behind it

Run the survey at an address on your own domain, which Emergent includes and bills in credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and reuse it next cycle.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Teams Run Their Pay Surveys
fields.tab_content_1:
No job published with fewer than 5 firms

Ridgeline Logistics Council runs one salary survey a year. Member firms enter base pay and headcount for 22 benchmark jobs, and a job publishes only when 5 or more firms report it. Warehouse supervisor drew 11 firms and published at a median of $68,400. Fleet safety manager drew 3 and stays held.
fields.tab_content_2:
A monthly salary sent back to the firm

Corlew Freight typed $6,250 as base salary for its full-time bookkeeper. The council sets a $30,000 floor for any full-time job, and anything lower goes back to the firm with the rule attached. The payroll lead saw a monthly number in an annual field and resubmitted $75,000 a year.
fields.tab_content_3:
Pay for 12 job classes, checked against 8 counties

Halvorsen County wants a peer comparison before bargaining opens. Its survey asks 8 neighboring counties for the top-step pay of 12 job classes. Deputy clerk tops out at $52,900 in Halvorsen, against a peer median of $57,000, a gap of $4,100. That line goes into the board packet.
fields.tab_content_4:
Who understands how their pay is set

Penbrook Software asked every employee about pay, and 186 answered anonymously, grouped by team. Asked whether they understand how their pay is set, 24 of 58 people in support agreed, against 50 of 64 in engineering. HR booked a session on pay ranges for the support team the next week.

fields.howto_title: How to Run a Compensation Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to run a compensation survey that collects comparable pay and publishes figures you can defend.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the jobs you will benchmark
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Describe each job in a few lines
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Decide which pay figures to collect
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Put a range on every pay field
fields.howto_step_1_des: Choose jobs that most participants employ and whose duties rarely change, such as warehouse supervisor or bookkeeper. Leave out one-of-a-kind roles, since too few firms will report them to publish. List the jobs in your prompt, and Emergent drafts a section for each.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write what each job does, who it reports to, and how many people it manages. The ERC guide to compensation surveys says to match positions by job description rather than title. One firm's coordinator can do the work another firm calls manager.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask for base salary, target bonus, headcount, and the date the pay took effect for each job. Skip anything a participant would have to work out by hand, like total cash for the year. Every extra calculation is a reason to abandon the survey halfway.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Give each pay field a floor and a ceiling, such as $30,000 and $400,000 for a full-time base salary. An entry outside the range returns to the participant for a fix before it can move a median. Review the ranges once the first answers come in.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Test it with one member firm
fields.howto_step_5_des: Before the invite goes out, ask one firm to submit real figures for three jobs. Check that each row lands in the table under the right job, then enter a monthly salary on purpose and confirm the floor catches it.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Tell firms what they get back
fields.howto_step_6_des: Promise every participant a report on each job that clears your publishing rule, and send it only to firms that submitted. Mercer makes the same offer: participants in its US compensation planning survey receive the results for free when they publish.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Show the spread, not only the median
fields.howto_step_7_des: Report the 25th and 75th percentile beside the median for every published job, so a participant can choose where it wants to pay. Keep each firm out of view: members see the aggregates, never another firm's row.

faq_plan.a: A compensation survey is a report of what a defined group of employers pay for a defined set of jobs over a defined period. Each employer submits pay for jobs matched to shared descriptions. The publisher returns medians and percentiles, and every participant sees where its own pay sits.

faq_plan.q: How to create a compensation survey?
faq_plan.ref: how to create a compensation survey
faq_plan.a: List the jobs, the pay figures you need, and who will answer, then describe all of it in one prompt. Emergent's AI survey builder drafts the questions and the table that stores each entry. Add rules later, like a salary floor or a deadline reminder, with a follow-up prompt.

faq_plan.q: What is the purpose of compensation surveys?
faq_plan.ref: what is the purpose of compensation surveys
faq_plan.a: Compensation surveys show what other employers pay for the same work. HR teams use the figures to set pay ranges, size the raise budget, and price a new role before posting it. When you run your own survey on Emergent, every raw entry stays in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: How do organizations benefit from using compensation surveys?
faq_plan.ref: how do organizations benefit from using compensation surveys
faq_plan.a: Organizations benefit by pricing jobs against market pay instead of guesses. The survey shows which jobs sit below the market, which is the first place to look when a role stays open for months. Pay figures say where you stand but not why people stay, and an employee engagement survey answers the second question.

faq_plan.q: How to use compensation survey data?
faq_plan.ref: how to use compensation survey data
faq_plan.a: Match each of your jobs to the survey job with the closest description, then compare your pay with the percentiles. Move older figures forward by your expected raise budget, since data collected in March is stale by a January review. Pick the percentile you pay at before you look at any one salary.

faq_plan.q: What questions should a compensation survey include?
faq_plan.a: For a market survey, ask each participant for its industry, region, and headcount, then for each job: the number of people in it, the range minimum and maximum, and actual pay. For an internal survey, ask staff whether they understand how pay is set and find it fair. An employee satisfaction survey can carry both. Keep compensation survey questions to figures payroll already holds.

faq_plan.q: Where can I get a compensation survey template?
faq_plan.a: You can generate one. Describe your participants and job list in a prompt, and Emergent drafts a compensation survey template with a section per job and the pay fields each one needs. For departing staff, pay questions fit better in an exit survey, where people say whether pay drove the decision to leave.

faq_plan.q: What are some compensation survey examples?
faq_plan.a: Three compensation survey examples cover the ground. A market salary survey is filled in by firms in one industry or region, and an executive pay survey asks only about senior leaders. An internal survey asks staff how they see their own pay, comparing teams inside one company rather than employers.

faq_plan.q: How to conduct a compensation survey?
faq_plan.ref: How to conduct a compensation survey?

prov.original: How to conduct a compensation survey?

faq_plan.a: Pick the employers whose pay you compete with, name one contact at each, and give them three to four weeks to submit. Chase anyone missing a week before the close, check every entry against your ranges, and publish only aggregates. Emergent builds the reminders into the survey, with every submission in one table and no cap on responses.

faq_plan.q: How to read and interpret compensation survey reports?
faq_plan.ref: how to read and interpret compensation survey reports
faq_plan.a: Start with the sample behind each job: how many organizations reported it. Treat a figure built from a handful of firms as a rough guide. Then read the percentiles. The 50th is the middle of the market, and the gap between the 25th and 75th shows how widely employers pay for that job. Check whether a column is base salary or total cash before comparing it with your own pay.

plan.angle: Nine of the top 10 are survey vendors and agencies selling or describing finished salary data (Mercer, Pearl Meyer, Gallagher, Croner, BLS, CalHR). None shows how to run one: how the jobs are matched, what gets collected, how a bad entry is caught, or when a figure is safe to publish. This page answers the definition and vendor questions in the FAQ, then shows four compensation surveys built from a prompt: a trade council\u0027s member salary survey that holds thin jobs, the submission check that sends a monthly figure back, a county\u0027s peer survey that lands in a board packet, and an internal pay-clarity survey split by department. The employee benefits and satisfaction siblings own benefits and job satisfaction; this page owns pay data.
tab_stories: Ridgeline Logistics Council collects base pay for 22 benchmark jobs from its member firms and publishes a job only when 5 or more firms report it, so fleet safety manager, reported by 3 firms, stays held while warehouse supervisor, reported by 11, publishes at a median of $68,400.

Corlew Freight enters $6,250 as a bookkeeper\u0027s base salary, under the $30,000 floor the council set for a full-time job, so the entry goes back to its payroll lead, who corrects it to $75,000 a year.

Halvorsen County asks 8 neighboring counties for the top-step pay of 12 job classes, and the report shows its deputy clerk at $52,900 against a peer median of $57,000, 7% below, a line that goes into the board packet before bargaining.
Penbrook Software asks its staff whether they understand how their pay is set, and 41% of support agrees against 78% of engineering, so HR books a session on pay ranges for the support team.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a Compensation Survey and Own the Pay Data', title 'Compensation Survey Builder for Pay Data | Emergent' and hero 'Build a compensation survey that matches jobs by description, checks each salary entered, and saves it to a database you own.' state the whole job; howto_description is one sentence.

intent.evidence: The SERP is vendors and agencies selling salary data. The page answers what one is (FAQ 1), who offers them (FAQ 10: Mercer, Pearl Meyer, BLS), how to conduct and use one (FAQ 9, FAQ 5, the 7-step how-to), and shows four surveys built from a prompt. The AMBER pay-feedback angle is carried by tab 4 and FAQ 6 (note).

specificity.evidence: Comp-practitioner vocabulary: benchmark jobs matched by description, publishing threshold of 5 firms, top-step pay, peer median, 25th and 75th percentile, effective date.

openers.evidence: Body paragraphs open on full sentences: 'Ridgeline Logistics Council runs one salary survey a year.', 'Corlew Freight typed $6,250...', 'Choose jobs that most participants employ...'. The fragment subheading is a note.

craft.evidence: Mostly one idea per sentence ('Fleet safety manager drew 3 and stays held.'); tacked-on clauses in FAQ 4 and step 7 are notes.

voice.evidence: Operator voice: 'Skip anything a participant would have to work out by hand, like total cash for the year.' No AI tells.

truth.evidence: Third-party lines match their quotes: ERC definition and 'match positions by job description rather than title'; Mercer 'annual increase budgets, structure adjustments and incentive usage' and 'receive the results for free when they publish'; Pearl Meyer 'more than 80 executive positions' (its page also offers 'Purchase Report', so 'sell them' holds); BLS NCS. Emergent lines map to prompt-build, database-owned, alerts, no-caps, custom-domain, code-export. Numbers: 6,250 x 12 = 75,000; 57,000 - 52,900 = 4,100 (7%); 64+18+46+58 = 186; 24/58 = 41%, 50/64 = 78%.

distinct.evidence: Owns pay data; no sibling primary (employee satisfaction, employee benefits, engagement survey) headlined; engagement, exit and 360 survey only linked.

faq.evidence: 10 on-topic questions answered first-sentence; hub link in item 2; locked items 1, 9, 10 match the skeleton; all four secondaries carried; no brand in a question (brands only in the FAQ 10 answer).

images.evidence: Contact sheet matches the tabs: warehouse supervisor 11 firms $68,400 Published, fleet safety manager 3 Held with '5 needed to publish'; $6,250 sent back under the $30,000 floor, $75,000 a year; deputy clerk $52,900 vs $57,000, gap $4,100, -7%; Support 24 of 58 (41%) vs Engineering 50 of 64, 186 answered.
